Software Engineering for AI-Driven Science
Lukas Twist∗, Xinjian Wu ∗, Jingzhi Gong ∗, Shuyin Ouyang ∗, Ying Xiao ∗, Benedetta Donato ‡,
Yaoqi Guo†, Zhenpeng Chen §, Leonardo Mariani ‡, Helen Yannakoudakis ∗, Jie M. Zhang ∗
∗King's College London, UK †Nanyang Technological University, Singapore ‡University of Milano-Bicocca, Italy §Tsinghua University, China
Abstract—AI has made significant contributions to scientific
discovery. Autonomous agents can now independently analyse
complex problems, design experiments, write and execute code,
analyse findings, and derive scientific conclusions. Nevertheless,
errors in AI-generated code, experimental procedures, or evi-
dence interpretation can lead to invalid research conclusions,
undermining the reliability and reproducibility of automated
scientific discovery. In this vision paper, we propose Software
Engineering for AI-Driven Science

path from a scientific question to a scientific claim as a
sequence of transformations. This is not intended as another
software lifecycle model, but as a view of how scientific intent
is transformed through software into executable artefacts,
evidence, and ultimately claims, making the full path an SE
assurance problem. Intent is operationalised into an experi-
mental design; its computational components are realised in
software; the experiment is carried out in a concrete setting;
execution produces evidence; and that

as a scientific claim. These transformations motivate the six
assurance stages shown in Fig. 1.
Intent captures the scientific question and assumptions;
experimental design specifies methods, baselines, subjects or
datasets, controls, metrics, and analysis procedures, including
any computational workflow; implementation realises the com-
putational components of that design in software; execution
carries out the experiment, potentially combining computation,
physical experiments, and human-participant studies; evidence
captures the resulting observations; and claim interprets those
observations scientifically. Software may coordinate execution
without automating every step. The abstraction is intentionally
domain-general, but the stages are distinct because each rep-
resents a different artefact or decision boundary with different
properties to assure.

Recent systems provide documented failures at every stage.
Some areloud, such as crashes or uncontrolled execution;
others aresilent, where the workflow completes successfully
while the procedure, evidence, or claim is wrong. Rather than
attempt a broad analysis across an ill-defined population of
AI-driven scientific systems, we focus on six illustrative cases
spanning the chain. Our aim is not to estimate prevalence, but
to groundSE4AI4Sciin observed failures: each case shows
where existing checks can fall short and motivates a distinct
assurance challenge for AI-driven science.

FORSOFTWAREENGINEERING
The failures above point to assurance problems that become
more difficult when autonomous agents participate in the
scientific process. Existing software-engineering techniques
provide strong foundations, but they were not designed for
systems that can choose methods, modify workflows, act on
intermediate results, and interpret their own evidence. The
six stage-specific questions therefore motivate five broader
research directions.IntentandExperimental Designtogether
motivate preserving scientific intent and method constraints;
Implementationmotivates testing science when the correct
answer is unknown;Executionmotivates assuring autonomous
scientific decisions; andEvidenceandClaimtogether motivate
tracing evidence into claims. A fifth, cross-cutting direction—
benchmarking scientific assurance—provides a common basis
for evaluating progress across all six

Building the SE4AI4Sci Community:We have created
and commit to maintainingawesome-se4ai4sci, 1 a cu-
rated repository of work relevant toSE4AI4Sci. We seeded
it from this paper's references, database searches, snow-
balling [39], and existing curated lists, screening candidates
against documented inclusion criteria. Organised around the
six stages of theScientific Assurance Chain, the repository
separates documented failures fromSE4AI4Sciwork and
includes related agents, benchmarks, and foundations. We
intend it to lower the barrier to entering the area, expose gaps,
and support a future systematic survey and taxonomy.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: No empirical benchmark outcome or optimized system is reported, so no independent corroboration is required.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Qualitative alignment of the proposed Scientific Assurance Chain against six documented failure cases drawn from published AI-for-science literature.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; this is a vision and framework paper that does not train, tune, select, or otherwise adapt a model or algorithm.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The claims are properly scoped to framing an emerging research area and structuring research challenges; no empirical algorithmic performance improvements are claimed.
primary.evaluation_assessment: As a vision and framework paper, it validates its conceptual model by mapping six concrete, documented failure modes from recent agentic discovery literature to specific break points in the chain, providing appropriate qualitative validation for a position paper.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The paper does not report an empirical quantitative benchmark outcome requiring independent corroboration.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Qualitative analysis and alignment against six documented real-world AI-for-science failure modes in published literature.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; the paper is a vision and position framework that does not train, optimize, or tune a model or algorithm.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly note that the failure cases serve as illustrative examples rather than an exhaustive prevalence estimate, leaving systematic multi-discipline taxonomies and benchmark development for future work.
primary.method_assessment: The manuscript conceptualizes a 6-stage lifecycle (Intent, Experimental Design, Implementation, Execution, Evidence, Claim) along with associated assurance obligations, linking software engineering tools like requirements engineering, metamorphic testing, and provenance tracking to stage-specific risks.
primary.quality_rationale: The paper provides a coherent, well-structured framework clearly distinguishing each phase of AI-driven scientific assurance, properly positioning related work, and setting concrete, actionable research challenges without unwarranted claims.
primary.scoped_contribution: This vision paper defines Software Engineering for AI-Driven Science (SE4AI4Sci), introducing the Scientific Assurance Chain framework to track transitions across scientific workflows, grounding challenges in documented failure cases, and setting an agenda for software-engineering mechanisms in autonomous research.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper provides a coherent, well-structured framework clearly distinguishing each phase of AI-driven scientific assurance, properly positioning related work, and setting concrete, actionable research challenges without unwarranted claims.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly note that the failure cases serve as illustrative examples rather than an exhaustive prevalence estimate, leaving systematic multi-discipline taxonomies and benchmark development for future work.
